payload.name: exec
payload.input:
const r = await tools.exec_command({cmd:"cat > enrichment/bible/work/s087/discovery/prepared-20261005/87_12/luna/list.tsv <<'EOF'
strong	tevrat	paralel	WLC:Exod.3.2	Moses and burning bush	Exodus opens with Moses seeing a bush aflame yet unconsumed, a fire that draws him toward revelation; the Qur'anic Moses likewise sees a fire while traveling, but the scene's signal leads into a different account of his call.
strong	tevrat	paralel	WLC:Exod.3.4	Moses called from the fire	God calls Moses from within the burning bush after he approaches it; this makes nearness to fire the threshold of a divine summons, unlike the condemned person's inescapable entry into the great fire.
strong	tevrat	motif	WLC:Exod.13.21	Night fire as guide	A pillar of fire leads Israel by night; it supplies the concrete scriptural counterpart to the commentary's distant fire as a route-finding sign, while its fire guides rather than consumes.
strong	tevrat	motif	WLC:Zech.3.2	Brand rescued from fire	Joshua is called a brand snatched from fire amid Satan's accusation; the image sharply contrasts the commentary's person fixed in fire with one taken out of it by divine rebuke.
strong	tevrat	motif	WLC:Isa.66.24	Undying worm and unquenched fire	Isaiah shows the corpses of rebels where worm and fire do not cease; the next Qur'anic verse says the entrant neither dies nor lives, and Isaiah's corpses make the difference between the images worth keeping visible.
strong	incil	motif	SBLGNT:Mark.9.48	Worm does not die; fire is not quenched	Jesus cites the undying worm and unquenched fire for Gehenna; alongside the Qur'anic entrant who neither dies nor lives, this gives an explicit neighboring-scripture formulation of punishment beyond ordinary death.
strong	tevrat	motif	WLC:Mal.3.19	Furnace burns the arrogant	The day burns arrogant evildoers like stubble and leaves neither root nor branch; this joins the commentary's great fire to pride and final judgment, not simply to a larger physical flame.
strong	tevrat	motif	WLC:Isa.33.14	Who can dwell with devouring fire?	Isaiah's sinners ask who can live with devouring fire and everlasting burnings; the question directly frames the commentary's defining issue of what kind of person can abide in fire.
medium	tevrat	motif	WLC:Isa.33.15	Righteousness answers the fire question	The following verse answers Isaiah's question with the one who walks righteously and speaks uprightly, then promises secure dwelling; it contrasts the Qur'anic wicked person's entry with an upright person able to dwell near divine fire.
strong	incil	motif	SBLGNT:Matt.3.12	Wheat gathered and chaff burned	John's winnowing separates wheat into the barn and burns chaff with unquenchable fire; it makes the commentary's two groups after admonition concrete as a sorting whose result is different fates.
strong	incil	motif	SBLGNT:Matt.25.41	Eternal fire assigned to the condemned	The king sends the cursed to eternal fire prepared for the devil and his angels; fire is the assigned end of a class identified in judgment, matching the commentary's person defined by his destination.
medium	incil	motif	SBLGNT:Matt.25.46	Eternal punishment set against life	Jesus pairs eternal punishment with eternal life as the two outcomes of judgment; this sharpens the Qur'anic contrast between the fire-bound person and the other person who prospers and prays.
strong	incil	motif	SBLGNT:Luke.16.24	A dead rich man suffers in flame	In the parable the rich man is dead yet conscious, tormented in flame and begging for water; it gives a specific image for enduring fiery suffering, while the Qur'anic following verse describes the state as neither death nor life.
strong	incil	motif	SBLGNT:Luke.16.26	No crossing out of the place of torment	Abraham says a fixed chasm prevents passage between the places of comfort and torment; this supplies a concrete account of the fire-bound person's inability to leave, like the commentary's gloss that yaslâ entails remaining with the fire.
strong	incil	motif	SBLGNT:Jude.1.7	Sodom as an example of eternal fire	Jude recalls Sodom and neighboring cities undergoing punishment of eternal fire; the shared judgment-by-fire story adds a scriptural precedent while the Qur'anic verse applies the fate to an unnamed individual.
strong	incil	motif	SBLGNT:Rev.14.9	Mark, worship, and fiery judgment	An angel warns that anyone worshipping the beast and receiving its mark will drink God's wrath in fire and sulfur; the commentary's fire-as-identifying brand thus meets a text where allegiance-mark and fiery fate are explicitly joined.
strong	incil	motif	SBLGNT:Rev.14.11	Smoke rises and the condemned have no rest	The smoke of torment rises forever and the worshippers of the beast have no rest day or night; this makes the commentary's abiding in fire a specific unending condition.
strong	incil	karsi_anlati	SBLGNT:Rev.20.14	The lake of fire is called the second death	Revelation names the lake of fire the second death, whereas the Qur'anic next verse says its entrant neither dies nor lives; the difference is a direct theological contrast in how fiery punishment is described.
medium	tevrat	motif	WLC:Deut.32.22	Wrath's fire reaches Sheol	Moses' song says divine anger kindles a fire that burns to Sheol below and consumes the land; its downward and encompassing reach gives a concrete cosmic scale to the commentary's great fire.
medium	tevrat	motif	WLC:Deut.4.24	God as consuming fire	Moses calls Israel's God a consuming fire and a jealous God; this locates fire also in divine presence and judgment, not only in the condemned person's destination.
medium	tevrat	motif	WLC:Exod.12.8	Passover meat roasted over fire	Hebrew צְלִי־אֵשׁ (roasted by fire), likely cognate with the source commentary's Arabic ص ل ي label, names Passover meat eaten at the meal; it preserves the cooking sense of the source's fire-verb family apart from punishment.
medium	tevrat	motif	WLC:Prov.6.27	Fire carried in the bosom	The proverb asks whether one can carry fire in the bosom without burning clothes; it gives a concrete counterpoint to controlled warming, showing that close contact with fire carries consequences.
medium	tevrat	motif	WLC:Prov.6.28	Walking on coals burns the feet	The proverb asks whether one can walk on hot coals without scorching the feet; it makes bodily exposure to fire the issue, rather than merely seeing or approaching a distant flame.
medium	tevrat	motif	WLC:Exod.3.4	Voice from the burning bush	When Moses turns aside, God calls from the bush; the fire first sought as a sign becomes a place of address, echoing the commentary's contrast between an approached fire that guides and one that traps.
medium	tevrat	motif	WLC:Lev.6.6	Altar fire must keep burning	The priestly law commands that fire remain continually lit on the altar; this is a persistent sacred fire maintained in worship, distinct from the punitive fire in which the commentary's person remains.
medium	tevrat	motif	WLC:Mal.3.2	Refiner's fire tests who can stand	The messenger's coming is compared to a refiner's fire, with the question who can endure the day; it connects fire's severity to a test of the person rather than only to destruction.
medium	tevrat	motif	WLC:Mal.3.3	Fire refines and purifies silver	The refiner sits to purify silver and the sons of Levi so they may offer rightly; this gives the commentary's metalworking fire a scriptural use that corrects and restores rather than merely burns.
medium	tevrat	motif	WLC:Dan.3.25	A fourth figure walks in the furnace	Nebuchadnezzar sees four men walking unbound in the furnace, with a divine-looking fourth; fire becomes the setting of protected presence, contrary to the bound person's suffering in the great fire.
medium	tevrat	motif	WLC:Dan.3.27	The furnace does not burn the faithful	Onlookers find that the men's bodies were unharmed and not a hair singed; this particular deliverance shows fire's force can be withheld, complementing the commentary's distinct fire of blessing and warmth.
medium	tevrat	motif	WLC:Isa.43.2	Passing through fire without being burned	God promises Israel that when they walk through fire they will not be scorched; the image reverses the commentary's entrant who must bear the fire's full heat and cannot leave.
medium	tevrat	soydas	WLC:Dan.6.11	Aramaic prayer ṣallē	The Aramaic verse says Daniel kneels and prays three times daily; its צלי prayer verb is a cognate of the source commentary's prayer-form صَلَّى, while the commentary carefully distinguishes that prayer root from the fire-verb ص ل ي.
medium	tevrat	motif	WLC:Ps.66.12	Tested through fire and brought out	The psalm says the people passed through fire and water before God brought them into abundance; fire names an ordeal one can survive, matching the commentary's secondary sense of suffering a hard trial.
medium	incil	motif	SBLGNT:1Cor.3.13	Fire reveals each person's work	Paul says the Day will disclose each person's work because fire tests what sort it is; like the commentary's fire that makes a person's identity legible, this fire exposes what the person has made.
medium	incil	motif	SBLGNT:1Cor.3.15	Saved through fire, with loss	Paul says a person's work may burn and he suffer loss, though he himself is saved as through fire; this provides a sharply contrary outcome to the one who remains inside punitive fire.
medium	incil	motif	SBLGNT:1Pet.1.7	Faith tested as gold by fire	Peter compares tested faith to gold refined by fire; the metaphor supplies a specific trial-and-refinement sense for the commentary's claim that the fire-verb can name undergoing hardship.
medium	incil	motif	SBLGNT:Heb.12.29	God is a consuming fire	Hebrews applies Moses' consuming-fire image to God; alongside the Qur'anic great fire, it keeps divine holiness and danger in view rather than treating fire only as a place.
medium	incil	motif	SBLGNT:2Pet.2.6	Sodom reduced to ashes as warning	Peter says God reduced Sodom and Gomorrah to ashes and made them an example of what comes to the ungodly; this joins remembered fire judgment to present warning, as the commentary calls the fire itself an admonition.
medium	tevrat	yorum_gelenegi	Genesis Rabbah 38:13	Abraham delivered from Nimrod's furnace	Genesis Rabbah expands Abraham's story with Nimrod throwing him into a furnace and God rescuing him; the tradition makes fire a test that reveals fidelity and grants rescue, not simply an identity assigned by punishment.
medium	tevrat	yorum_gelenegi	Rosh Hashanah 17a	Gehenna's punishment has a stated limit	The Talmud describes some sinners as judged in Gehenna for twelve months, after which bodies are consumed and souls burned; this later Jewish account contrasts with the Qur'anic description of a state in which the entrant neither dies nor lives.
medium	tevrat	yorum_gelenegi	Mishnah Avot 5:19	Abraham's and Balaam's disciples inherit different ends	The Mishnah classifies disciples by their traits and assigns Abraham's disciples the world to come but Balaam's disciples Gehinnom; it gives a Jewish interpretive example of a person's defining way of life determining the destination.
medium	tevrat	motif	WLC:Isa.43.2	Fire can accompany a protected journey	Isaiah's promise of safe passage through fire makes the fire a traversed environment rather than a final dwelling; this is a direct contrary image to the condemned person's abiding inside it.
medium	tevrat	motif	4 Ezra 7:36	Furnace of Gehenna opposite a place of rest	4 Ezra reveals the furnace of Gehenna opposite a place of rest and delight; it concretely pairs fiery punishment with the other destiny, as the commentary's surrounding verses divide people into two outcomes.
EOF", max_output_tokens:2000});
text(r.output);
